lesson.menu_desc: Reading about accents, native and non-native speakers, and how to start speaking again after years without practice: I used to... / I’m getting used to... -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- English Without Borders
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Caroline Teixeira Nomiyama | Lesson 8 -- English Without Borders
lesson.grammar_point: used to + verb (past habit: I used to study on Saturdays) x be used to + noun / -ing (familiar: I am used to working late) x get used to + noun / -ing (process: I am getting used to the accent)

listenings.text: When I moved from Sydney to Houston, I thought English was the easy part. English is my first language, right? Well, on my first day, I asked for a glass of water in a restaurant, and the waiter just looked at me. I didn't pronounce the r, and he didn't understand. It happened again and again. People were friendly, but I wasn't used to their accent, and they weren't used to mine. I felt a bit shy for the first time in my life. Now, after three years, I'm used to the Texas accent, and my colleagues are used to me. So every accent is just practice, even for native speakers.

I work in a law firm in Berlin, and we have clients in many countries. For years, I used to stay silent in international meetings. I understood everything, but I only took notes. I was afraid of making mistakes, with my accent and with my grammar. Then a partner told me something simple: nobody remembers your mistakes, but they remember if you never speak. So I tried two things. First, I prepare one question before every meeting. Second, I speak in the first ten minutes, before I get nervous. It wasn't easy at the start, but now I'm used to it, and I feel much more confident.

I'm from India, and I've worked as a tour guide in Kyoto for five years. When I arrived, I spoke English every day, but English in Japan was difficult for me. The rhythm was different, and some sounds changed. For example, many people added a small vowel at the end of words. At first, when I didn't understand, I used to smile and say yes. That was a mistake. Now I'm used to it. I ask people to repeat, and I listen to the rhythm and the important words, not every sound. I always tell tourists the same thing: it's normal to ask again. People are happy to help you.

paras: Ten years ago, Marina was a good student of English. She used to take a class every Saturday morning, and she used to get good grades. Then came university, then work, and English slowly disappeared from her life. Last year, on her honeymoon in Japan, she discovered the problem. She still understood a lot, but her English was rusty, and the accents were new to her. When people spoke to her, she smiled and let her husband answer. “I used to love English,” she says. “Suddenly I was too shy to say a word.”

Marina’s story is very common. Today, most people who speak English are not native speakers: there are about three non-native speakers for every native one. In an international meeting, you can hear ten different accents in one hour, from Tokyo to Texas. Nobody is used to all of them, and even native speakers need time to get used to a new accent. Researchers say that the problem is rarely the accent of the speaker. It is how many times the listener has heard it before.

So how do you start speaking again? First, accept that you will make mistakes. Everybody does, in every language. Second, choose clarity, not a perfect accent: if you pronounce the important words clearly, people will understand you. Third, speak up early in a meeting, before you get nervous. “At first it was strange,” Marina says. “Now I’m used to hearing my own voice in English, and I’m getting used to asking the questions. I’m not fluent yet, but I’m confident.”
